# Motivation

## Why this talk {.smaller}

- NAS (2009) and PCAST (2016): scientific validity of firearms examination has not been established
- Recent large-scale black-box validation studies have attempted to remedy this (Ames I and II, Hicklin et al)
- @cuellar2024methodological: literature search of 28 black-box validation studies
  - Found six flaws (A–F) present, with minor exceptions, in **every** study
  - Concluded: none of the existing studies can establish scientific validity
- @chin2026towards responded: a flaw in one study doesn't doom the whole evidence base
  - Draws on evidence-based medicine / systematic-review practice
  - Argues for a **cumulative** forensic science: openness, registration, meta-analysis


## The six flaws {.smaller}

| Flaw | Description | Cuellar et al. framing |
|---|---|---|
| A | Inadequate sample size | Exacerbates the other flaws |
| B | Non-representative sample (examiners, firearms, ammunition) | Damages the data |
| C | Non-representative testing conditions (contextual bias, known-test effects) | Damages the data |
| D | Inconclusives treated as correct or ignored | Fixable if raw responses available |
| E | Invalid or nonexistent uncertainty measures | Fixable if raw responses available |
| F | Missing data handled inappropriately | Fixable if missingness can be characterized |


## Where we agree with Chin et al.

- No single study is perfect
- Not every flaw has the same consequences
- Analytic shortcomings (D, E) may be **repairable after the fact** if the raw
  responses were recorded
- Imperfect studies are still useful for some purposes 
- We should not discourage data collection just because a study has flaws 

## Main point of disagreement: 

> The problem is not simply that the wrong quantity was reported. The problem is that the data needed to estimate the relevant quantity were never collected in the first place.

- Some flaws (B, C) operate on **study design and sampling**, not analysis
- No amount of reanalysis recovers information that was never observed
- **Claim of this talk:** the six flaws split into two qualitatively different
  buckets — remediable (fixable via reanalysis) and non-remediable (fixable
  only with new data)

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This is the thesis statement — say it out loud, slowly. Everything
after this slide is in service of defending this one claim.
:::

# The Remediable / Non-Remediable Distinction

## What "remediable" means here

Fix a target quantity (the **estimand**):

> the population-average examiner error rate (FPR / FNR), under casework-representative
> firearms, ammunition, examiners, and testing conditions

- **Remediable**: given the raw examiner-by-item responses, the estimand can
  still be validly estimated (possibly with extra assumptions / new analysis)
- **Non-remediable**: the sampled data cannot support the estimand, *regardless*
  of what analysis is applied to them

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Naming the estimand explicitly is what makes the rest of the flowchart
legible — don't skip this slide even though it feels abstract.
:::

2. Non-remediable flaw example

## Approach: simulation study

- We can't go back and observe the "true" error rate for the 28 studies
- A simulation with a **known ground truth** lets us show, precisely, what each flaw does to a study's conclusions
- Same generative model powers both case studies

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::



## Data generating model

- Each item $i$ has a latent difficulty $d_i \sim N(0, \sigma_d^2)$
- Each examiner $j$ has a latent skill $s_j \sim N(0, \sigma_s^2)$ **and** a latent tendency to call items inconclusive $\tau_j \sim N(0, \tau_j^2)$
- Pairing item $i$ with examiner $j$ creates a decision challenge: $c_{ij} = d_i - s_j$
    - this becomes an "offset" from the overall estimand


## Response probabilities {.smaller}

Target estimand: overall population FPR or FNR or IR

A harder item or a weaker examiner makes the challenge larger, which pushes up both the chance of an error and the chance of an inconclusive call on the log-odds scale: 

$\pi_{ij}^{err} = P(\text{FP}) = \text{expit}[\text{logit(FPR)} + c_{ij}]$

$\pi_{ij}^{inc} = P(\text{Inconclusive}) = \text{expit}[\text{logit(IR)} + 0.5 \cdot c_{ij} + \tau_j]$

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. The 0.5 weight on $c_{ij}$ in the inconclusive term and the 0.95
cap are both ad hoc constants in the current code — flag as a limitation if
asked, and put a sensitivity analysis on the to-do list.
:::

## The response, formally {.smaller}

$e(\cdot)$ denotes an error and $c(\cdot)$ denotes a correct response. $G_i$ indicates ground truth (SS or DS)

$$
R_{ij} \mid G_i, c_{ij}, \tau_j \;\sim\; 
\begin{cases}
e(G_i) & \text{w.p. } \pi^{err}_{ij} \\
\text{inconclusive} & \text{w.p. } \pi^{inc}_{ij} \\
c(G_i) & \text{w.p. } 1 - \pi^{err}_{ij} - \pi^{inc}_{ij}
\end{cases}
$$

independently across $(i,j)$ given the latent variables above.

## Calibrating to real studies

- Baseline rates retuned against a benchmark reconstructed from
  @cuellar2024methodological's bounding-procedure algebra for Monson,
  Smith, and Bajic (2023a) — see `icfis/analysis.qmd`
- Also anchored to Scurich et al. (2025)'s blind-vs-known-test
  inconclusive rates (39.3% / 56.4%) and Ames II's 0%–62% "hard"-comparison
  range across individual Beretta pistols
- Result: FPR/FNR land within ~2x of the benchmark (down from 3.5–4.4x
  before retuning) — but the model's one shared `inconclusive_rate`
  parameter **cannot** reproduce the benchmark's same-source vs.
  different-source inconclusive-rate asymmetry: a known, ~13-point
  residual gap in opposite directions, not fixable without giving the two
  ground-truth categories separate baselines

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. This slide doubles as a credibility signal — show the audience
you're not hand-waving the parameters, *and* that you know exactly where
the model still falls short. If pressed on "how well calibrated is this,
really?": good on FPR/FNR, honest known miss on the inconclusive
asymmetry specifically, deliberately not patched because fixing it means
changing the response-probability equation already used throughout the
talk (see icfis/analysis.qmd's "Retuning the baseline rates" section for
the full derivation).
:::


# Case Study 1: A Remediable Flaw

## Setup: inconclusive handling (Flaw D)

- Black-box studies handle inconclusive responses inconsistently — excluded,
  folded into "correct," or otherwise treated as if they don't affect the
  error rate
- @cuellar2024methodological recommend a bounding procedure instead: recode
  every inconclusive as an identification, then as an elimination, and
  report **both** recomputed error rates as a range
- Sharper point from working through the algebra: for how Monson, Smith, and
  Bajic (2023a) define these rates, the number a study **reports** already
  equals one of the two bounds — it is not a neutral middle ground
- Claim: this is *remediable* — both numbers come from the same raw
  responses, recomputed after the fact

::: {.notes}
~1 min. The "reported = one of the bounds" point is the hook — it means the
commonly-cited error rate was never a best estimate, it was already the
optimistic end of a range nobody reported the other end of.
:::

## Simulation design

- Same DGP as the rest of the talk, at the retuned defaults, under the
  study's actual incomplete design (50 examiners, 30 of 300 items each)
- For each simulated study, compute both numbers from the same raw
  responses:
  - **Reported**: identifications / all different-source cases (and the
    same-source analog for the false negative rate)
  - **Worst case**: recode every inconclusive as the error-favoring label,
    recompute
- Repeat across 100 replicate studies to check the gap is a stable pattern,
  not a fluke of one random draw

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min.
:::

## Results

- One example study: FPR **1.3% → 42.1%**, FNR **3.0% → 38.9%** — same raw
  responses, same study, wildly different numbers depending on a reporting
  choice made after data collection
- Across 100 replicate studies (means): FPR **1.6% → 38.7%**, FNR
  **3.3% → 40.4%** — the gap holds up, it's not one unlucky draw
- [FIGURE: boxplots of reported vs. worst-case FPR/FNR across 100 studies,
  faceted by rate — see icfis/case_study_inconclusive.qmd]

::: {.notes}
~2 min. Lead with the one-study numbers (concrete, easy to say out loud),
then the 100-study means as the "this isn't a fluke" follow-up. The boxplot
figure should show both distributions barely overlapping.
:::

## Why this counts as remediable

- The fix required **no new data collection** — the same raw examiner-by-item
  responses already support both numbers; only how they're summarized
  changed
- This is exactly the kind of flaw Chin et al. are right about: a study with
  this flaw alone can still contribute to a cumulative evidence base, *once
  reanalyzed*

::: {.notes}
~0.5 min. Land the point before moving to the harder case.
:::

# Case Study 2: A Non-Remediable Flaw

## Setup: non-representative sampling (Flaw B)

- Precondition for validity: firearms, ammunition, and examiners must
  represent the **full spectrum of real casework** [@cuellar2024methodological]
- None of the 28 studies demonstrate this
- Chin et al.'s response: non-representative samples can still contribute to
  a cumulative literature if combined with other studies / moderator analysis

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::

## Two levels of variability

- Different firearm makes/models have different baseline difficulties
    - **Simulation:** choose 8 types

- Individual firearms *within* a make/model also have different difficulties
    - **Simulation:** assume a difficulty distribution for each firearm type; draw 5 firearms from that distribution

- 8 types $\times$ 5 of each type = 40 individual firearms used to generate test cases
    - Ames II: used ~30

## Three different "analysis" approaches:

1. **Biased estimate.** A convenience sample restricted to only two types (21% of casework by weight), 5 firearms each 
2. **The fix that could work.** A hypothetical better study covering all
   eight types (5 firearms each, not in population-correct proportions)
   with type recorded as a covariate — reweighting by the true population
   distribution afterward — Chin et al.'s "moderator" / big-team-science
   suggestion.
3. **The fix that doesn't exist.** Applying that same reweighting to the
   *actual* convenience sample from (1), which has zero data on the six
   unsampled types — 79% of the population's weight.

::: {.notes}
~2 min. This is the slide to get right — beat 2 is what keeps this honest
(we're not claiming reweighting is impossible in principle), beat 3 is what
makes it non-remediable *for the existing studies*. The two-level design
(types, then firearms within type) mirrors how an actual black-box study
is built.
:::

## Results

500 replicate studies per scenario (checked for Monte Carlo stability
against a 100-replicate run — the estimates moved by at most 0.05
percentage points, so 100 would have been enough; 500 is used here as the
final, most precise number). True population rate: **FPR 2.13%,
FNR 3.67%**.

- Convenience sample (naive): FPR **0.40%**, FNR **0.77%** — roughly **5x
  too low** on both
- Convenience sample, "reweighted": FPR **0.44%**, FNR **0.86%** — still
  roughly **4.5x too low** — barely moved
- Full-coverage study, reweighted: FPR **2.27%**, FNR **3.98%** — within
  ~6–8% of truth on both — reweighting works, even with only 5 firearms
  sampled per type

::: {.notes}
~2 min. The punchline is the third bullet: the same statistically valid
reweighting procedure that worked in beat 2 does almost nothing here. Not
because it was done wrong — because there's nothing to weight. If asked
about the firearm-level noise, it's a secondary point: even a
well-designed study (full type coverage) still needs enough firearms
*per* type, echoing case study 1's sample-size point one level down.
:::

## Why this counts as non-remediable

- No statistical procedure applied to *this* dataset can recover the
  population-average estimand — reweighting is valid and
  works, even accounting for within-model firearm sampling noise; the same
  procedure applied to the convenience sample fails, not from a math
  error, but because 79% of the population was never observed at the type
  level
- Fixing it requires **new data** collected under a design that
  characterizes the target population — not a different analysis of the
  same responses

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::

# Conclusion

## Takeaways

- Not all six flaws are alike — sorting them by *remediable vs. non-remediable*
  clarifies exactly where Chin et al.'s cumulative-science argument applies
- **Remediable** (A, D, E, and F with assumptions): reanalysis of existing
  data can recover a valid estimate 
- **Non-remediable** (B, C): the target quantity was never within reach of
  the sampled data — no reanalysis fixes this

::: {.notes}
~1 min.
:::

## Recommendations

- Report raw, examiner-by-item responses (not just summary error/inconclusive rates) 
    - enables post-hoc correction of remediable flaws
- Pre-register sampling frames
    - characterize the target population of firearms / examiners *before* data collection
- Use cluster-aware / MRMC statistical methods designed for the dependence structure of validation studies


::: {.notes}
~1.5 min.
:::

## Appendix: contextual-bias extension (Flaw C) {.smaller}

Hawthorne shift, calibrated to Scurich et al. (2025) blind vs. known-test
inconclusive rates at the Houston Forensic Science Center:

$$
\delta_H = \operatorname{logit}(0.564) - \operatorname{logit}(0.393)
$$

Under the "known test" condition, the inconclusive-probability equation
gains one term (error probability is unaffected):

$$
\pi^{inc}_{ij}(\text{condition}) = \operatorname{expit}\Big[\operatorname{logit}(p_{IC}) + 0.5\,c_{ij} + \tau_j + \delta_H \cdot \mathbb{1}\{\text{condition} = \text{"known test"}\}\Big]
$$

::: {.notes}
Backup only. Use if asked why the FPR/FNR barely moved between conditions
in the case-study-2 exploratory run — the shift is currently uniform across
easy and hard items, which is exactly why it doesn't move conclusive-only
error rates much. That's a modeling choice worth revisiting, not a result.
:::

## Appendix: missingness extension (Flaw F) {.smaller}

$$
\text{is\_error}_{ij} = \mathbb{1}\{R_{ij} = e(G_i)\}
$$

$$
\pi^{miss}_{ij} = \operatorname{expit}\Big[\operatorname{logit}(0.05) + 0.8\,c_{ij} + 1.2\cdot\text{is\_error}_{ij} + 0.6\cdot\mathbb{1}\{R_{ij}=\text{"inconclusive"}\}\Big]
$$

$$
M_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi^{miss}_{ij}), \qquad
R^{obs}_{ij} = \begin{cases} R_{ij} & M_{ij} = 0 \\ \texttt{NA} & M_{ij} = 1 \end{cases}
$$

A missing-not-at-random mechanism: harder pairs, errors, and inconclusives
are all more likely to drop out, which is what biases naive (listwise-
deletion) error rates downward.

::: {.notes}
Backup only.
:::

## Appendix: what's left for CI coverage (Flaw E) {.smaller}

The individual-firearm random effect itself is **already built and in
use** — `make_firearm_population()` in `icfis/R/simulate_dgp_types.R`
gives each type $K$ individual firearms $k = 1, \dots, K$, each with
$f_k \sim N(0, \sigma_F^2)$, and case study 2 draws from it (5 firearms
per included type). What's *not* built is using that structure for CI
coverage:

- Case study 2 uses the firearm layer for a **bias** demonstration
  (does reweighting recover the population mean?) — it never constructs
  a confidence interval
- A Flaw E case study needs the same nested structure feeding an actual
  **interval-coverage** comparison: simulate many studies from a known
  true rate, compute a 95% CI three ways per study (naive Clopper–Pearson,
  cluster-robust, Gallas et al. 2009-style MRMC), and check what fraction
  of intervals actually contain the truth
- Responses for items sharing a firearm are **dependent** given $f_k$ —
  exactly what a naive interval ignores and a cluster-robust one accounts
  for; this is a different question from case study 2's, even though the
  generative structure is shared

::: {.notes}
Backup only — this is the concrete build item to report progress on if
asked "what's left to do." Don't say "not implemented" for the firearm
effect itself — it is; what's missing is the CI-coverage simulation loop
on top of it.
:::

## Appendix: is the "5x" just an artifact of our parameters? {.smaller}

Case study 2's `type_difficulty_sd`, `firearm_difficulty_sd`, and
`examiner_skill_sd` are uncalibrated. Checked a 3×3 grid (difficulty
heterogeneity × examiner heterogeneity, each Low/Medium/High; 50 replicate
studies per cell) — see `icfis/sensitivity_nonrepresentative.qmd`.

- **Bias ratio scales strongly with difficulty heterogeneity**: convenience
  sample is ~2–2.5x too low at Low, ~4–5x at Medium (the main case study's
  defaults), ~9–11x at High
- **Examiner heterogeneity has a real but much smaller effect** — moves the
  ratio only modestly across the same range
- **The qualitative story holds at all 9 settings tested**: full-coverage
  reweighted stays within 0.85x–1.31x of truth everywhere; convenience
  "reweighted" never climbs out of 0.10x–0.62x
- **Conclusion**: the specific multiplier ("5x") is not an empirical claim
  — it moves with unvalidated assumptions. The *direction* and the
  reweighting-works/fails distinction don't.

::: {.notes}
Backup only. Pull this up if asked "isn't 5x just an artifact of your
parameter choices?" — yes, the number is; the direction and mechanism
aren't. That's the whole slide in one sentence if time is short.
:::
